input:
In a countercurrent heat exchanger, the temperature difference that drives heat from one stream to the other is not the same at the two ends of the unit, and a single representative value is needed before the exchanger can be sized. The log-mean temperature difference, $\Delta T_{lm}$, is precisely that representative value. Consider an exchanger in which a process stream is cooled from 200 °C to 150 °C while the cooling water that serves it enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. Because the flow is countercurrent, the ends of the exchanger pair the streams in a particular way: at one end, the entering process stream faces the leaving water, and at the other end, the leaving process stream faces the entering water. Working through those pairings, the terminal differences come out at 125 K at the hot end and 110 K at the cold end. The log-mean temperature difference is then defined by the relation

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the hot and cold ends. Placing the two terminal differences into this relation gives a log-mean temperature difference of 117.3 K. It is worth noticing where that value sits: between the two terminal differences, and closer to the smaller of them, which is exactly where a logarithmic mean of two unequal quantities is expected to fall. The value rests on the assumptions that accompany it, namely that the overall coefficient stays constant along the exchanger and that neither stream changes phase; under those conditions, the log-mean value is the driving force the sizing calculation requires. The countercurrent pairing is what gives those two differences their meaning, since each one is read across the same end of the unit rather than along a single stream.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream with water, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is the mean driving force used in the sizing relation. Calculate $\Delta T_{lm}$ from the terminal temperatures. The process stream cools from 200 °C to 150 °C, and the water enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. Countercurrent flow pairs the entering process stream with the leaving water at the hot end, and the leaving process stream with the entering water at the cold end. The terminal differences are 125 K at the hot end and 110 K at the cold end. The log-mean temperature difference is defined by

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the hot and cold ends. Substitution of the two terminal differences gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 117.3 K. The value lies between the two terminal differences and nearer the smaller one; a logarithmic mean of two unequal positive quantities has that position, and the position is the check on the calculation. An arithmetic mean of the same two differences would sit higher and would overstate the driving force over most of the exchanger length. The result assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream. The log-mean construction is limited to those conditions: a stream that changes phase holds its temperature over part of the length, and the driving force in that part is not described by the terminal differences in the same way. The two terminal differences are not interchangeable in the construction. Each belongs to its own end of the exchanger, and pairing the streams wrongly would produce differences that describe an arrangement the unit does not have. Countercurrent flow keeps the difference between the streams more nearly even along the length than the alternative arrangement, and the log-mean value summarises that profile for the sizing relation.
